## About this session



::: {.callout-tip collapse="false" appearance="default" icon="true"}
## Session resources
+ you don't need any infrastructure apart from an R setup
+ see the setup chunk below for packages
+ you should have a reasonable working knowledge of R and, specifically, dplyr
:::

## Setup

Create a new project, install packages if needed, attach the stringr, tidytext, and dplyr packages, and create some simple data:

```{r}
# install.packages("dplyr")
# install.packages("dtplyr")
# install.packages("dbplyr")
# install.packages("palmerpenguins")
# install.packages("DBI")

library(dplyr)
library(dtplyr)
library(dbplyr)
library(palmerpenguins)

```

## What?

+ dplyr is great! Easy to read and write, nicely compatible with other R tools, with a chunky user-base and nice docs
+ dplyr is also a) slow and b) holds your data in memory
+ that means that when your data gets big (or complicated, or remote,...) dplyr becomes slow and annoying
+ the dream: write dplyr, but *execute something else* more capable of tackling the big data stuff
+ both dtplyr and dbplyr are both flavours of *execute something else* while writing dplyr
  + [dtplyr](https://dtplyr.tidyverse.org/articles/translation.html) = write dplyr, run [data.table](https://r-datatable.com/)
  + [dbplyr](https://dbplyr.tidyverse.org/) = write dplyr, run [SQL](https://www.w3schools.com/sql/)

## dtplyr

Why not just write data.table directly? Largely because it's very unlike ordinary R code:

```{r}
library(data.table)

peng_dt <- data.table(penguins)
peng_dt[island == "Dream"] # filter
peng_dt[,.(bill_length_mm)] # select
peng_dt[,bill_length_mm] # pull or $
peng_dt[,.N, island] # count
```


It's actually a great system if you have the time to spend getting comfortable with it: really a very concise way of writing SQL-ish expressions as we explore in [our training session on the topic](r_training/intro_data_table.html). But data.table code is hard to improvise, and it does take a bit of time and practice to get comfortable working in this way, especially if you've spent lots of time writing nice literate tidyverse code.

Enter dtplyr where we get to do things in data.table by learning three functions:

```{r}
peng_dtp <- dtplyr::lazy_dt(penguins) # create a dtplyr object

peng_dtp |>
  as_tibble() # if you need to get your results back as a proper tibble

peng_dtp |>
  collect() # similarly, returns a tibble
```

Otherwise you can largely just start plugging in dplyr code:

```{r}
peng_dtp |>
  filter(island == "Dream")

peng_dtp |>
  select(bill_length_mm)

peng_dtp |>
  pull(bill_length_mm)

peng_dtp |>
  count(island)
```

There are also some non-dplyr bits of tidyverse to play with too - check the [reference](https://dtplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/index.html):

```{r}
peng_dtp |>
  # select() |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(contains("mm"))
```


If you want to find out what's going on in ~~Narnia~~ data.table land, you can use `show_query()`

```{r}
peng_dtp |>
  count(island) |>
  show_query()
```

This is pretty interesting, and a delightfully lazy way to brush up on your data.table syntax:

```{r}
peng_dtp |>
  filter(island == "Dream") |>
  select(island, bill_length_mm) |>
  mutate(bill_length_rods = bill_length_mm / 5029.2) |>
  show_query()

```


```{r}
peng_dtp_inter_nc <- peng_dtp |>
  mutate(bill_vol = bill_length_mm * bill_depth_mm) 

peng_dtp_inter <- peng_dtp |>
  mutate(bill_vol = bill_length_mm * bill_depth_mm) |>
  compute() # intermediate assignment

waldo::compare(peng_dtp_inter_nc, peng_dtp_inter)
```

## dbplyr

dbplyr takes a similar approach to dtplyr, but has much more flexibility about source data. You can easily e.g. connect to a remote server or similar using DBI. To keep this session manageable, we'll create an in-memory SQLite database as a demonstration of how dbplyr might be used to manage large datasets in R:

```{r}
con <- DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), dbname = ":memory:") # create an object containing details of how to connect to an in-memory db

copy_to(con, penguins, "pengs") # connect, and add the penguins dataset as a table called pengs
```

We could access this db directly using SQL queries with a bit of help from the DBI package:

```{r}
con |> 
  DBI::dbGetQuery('SELECT * FROM pengs WHERE island == "Dream" LIMIT 5') # filter to keep the preview a sensible length

con |> 
  DBI::dbGetQuery('SELECT bill_length_mm FROM pengs LIMIT 5') # select

con |>
  DBI::dbGetQuery('SELECT island, count(*) as n FROM pengs GROUP BY island')
```

Again, SQL is great if you have time to learn it properly - although writing SQL queries nested inside brackets is pretty nasty - but for occasional use (or learning) dbplyr is even better. Confusingly, our core function comes from the dplyr package - `dplyr::tbl()` - which grabs data from our database, and allows us to use ordinary dplyr tools to modify it:

```{r}
tbl(con, "pengs") |>
  filter(island == "Dream") # to return a db preview
```

That's a preview - see e.g. the `??` number of rows. We do need to add a `dplyr::collect()` to turn that preview back into a proper tibble:
```{r}
tbl(con, "pengs") |>
  filter(island == "Dream") |>
  collect() # to return a proper tibble
```

Like `dtplyr::show_query`, we can see how dbplyr translates our code into SQL:

```{r}
tbl(con, "pengs") |>
  filter(island == "Dream") |>
  select(species) |>
  dplyr::show_query() # for L&D purposes
```

You can also see [the query plan](https://www.sqlite.org/eqp.html) to understand how your query is being implemented:

```{r}
tbl(con, "pengs") |>
  filter(island == "Dream") |>
  select(species) |>
  dplyr::explain()
```

While our earlier examples have returned tibbles, we can also return a new SQL table. Here, we create a new table named `dream_pengs`:

```{r}
tbl(con, "pengs") |>
  filter(island == "Dream") |>
  select(species, bill_depth_mm) |>
  dplyr::compute(name = "dream_pengs")
```

We can then query that new table:

```{r}
tbl(con, "dream_pengs") |>
  collect()
```

In addition to the `copy_to` approach that we explored earlier, we can also build new database objects in our R environment. That's a two-step process: create a [local lazy tibble](https://dbplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/tbl_lazy.html) (named `new_peng`):

```{r}
new_peng <- copy_inline(con, tibble(species = "Humboldt", bill_depth_mm = 31))

new_peng

new_peng |>
  class()
```

Then insert that lazy tibble into our database table. Here, we'll use `compute` again to create a new summarised table:

```{r}
rows_insert(tbl(con, "dream_pengs"), new_peng, conflict = "ignore") |>
  count(species) |>
  compute(name = "species_pengs")
```

```{r}
tbl(con, "species_pengs") |>
  collect()
```
